raw_response:
I've been farming these 5 mu for 25 years now — since I was 20. My father farmed this same land before me, and we’ve always done wheat-maize double cropping, same as most folks in Quzhou. I’m 45 now, finished middle school, and I know enough to understand what the extension agent says, but I also know that what works in the textbook doesn’t always work in my field.

With only 5 mu and five mouths to feed — my wife, my aging parents, and two kids (one works off-farm in Shijiazhuang, the other is still in school) — every yuan matters. My son sends some money back when he can, but I can’t count on it for farm inputs. I’ve got about 3,500 yuan saved for this year’s inputs, so I need to be careful. I’m not going to gamble on fancy new seeds or extra fertilizer just to squeeze out a few more jin. I’d rather have cash in my pocket for emergencies.

**Wheat:** I’ll plant around October 10th, right after the National Day holiday when the soil is still warm. I saved seed from last year’s harvest — a local improved variety that does well here, not the most expensive hybrid but reliable. I’ll mix in a little new seed, maybe 60 yuan per mu worth, to keep the vigor up. For fertilizer, the extension guy says 18 kg nitrogen per mu, but I’ve been doing 15 kg total for years and it’s been fine. I’ll put down 20 kg of compound fertilizer (15-15-15) at planting — that’s about 3 kg each of N, P, K. Then in March, at jointing, I’ll topdress with urea, about 12 kg per mu. If the wheat looks yellow, maybe I’ll add a bit more, but probably not. More fertilizer means less money for maize seed.

For irrigation, I’ve got the tube well, but the electricity meter runs fast. I’ll irrigate three times for wheat: once at green-up after winter, once at jointing, and once at heading in April if there’s no rain. If it rains well in spring, I might skip the last one and save 30-40 yuan. For pesticides, I’ll spray herbicide once in early spring, and if I see disease on the leaves, I’ll add a fungicide. My neighbor Lao Zhang skipped fungicide last year and lost yield, so I’d rather spend the 20 yuan and not risk it.

**Maize:** The key is speed. After wheat harvest in early June, I’ve got less than a week before I need to get maize in the ground. I hire a combine for wheat — 50 yuan per mu — because doing it by hand would take too long and I’d miss the planting window. Then I rotary till lightly and plant immediately. I’ll buy hybrid maize seed, about 4 kg per mu, costs around 50 yuan per mu. I learned my lesson trying saved maize seed years ago — the yield drop wasn’t worth it.

For maize fertilizer, I’ll put down compound at planting, about 15 kg per mu, then topdress urea at the big trumpet stage, about 10 kg per mu. That’s about 16 kg N total. Maize doesn’t need as much fussing as wheat. I’ll irrigate once or twice — July rains usually help, but if it’s dry at flowering, I’ll pump water. One irrigation for maize is almost certain. I’ll spray pre-emergence herbicide and that’s usually enough. Maybe insecticide if I see armyworm.

**Labor:** It’s mostly me and my wife. My dad can watch the pump. During wheat harvest and maize planting, the rush is bad — I might hire two people for a couple days at 100 yuan per day. That’s an extra 400-500 yuan, but missing the planting window costs more than that.

**Tradeoffs:** I thought about putting more nitrogen on wheat — maybe get 500 kg/mu instead of 450 kg/mu — but that extra 3 kg per mu across 5 mu is another 50-60 yuan in fertilizer, and wheat prices haven’t been great. I’d rather keep the cash. Same with maize — I could irrigate three times, but the well water isn’t free and the pump is old. Two times is enough if the rains cooperate.

I expect about 450 kg per mu for wheat and 500 kg per mu for maize if the weather is normal. Last year the spring was dry and wheat only did 400 kg/mu, so I’m being a bit conservative.
